## Abstract

This report examines the use of blood protein biomarkers to predict autism spectrum disorder (ASD), based on the findings of Hewitson et al. (2021). We first summarize the study's methodology and findings. We then replicate and evaluate an in-class predictive model using t-tests, random forest, and logistic regression. To explore potential improvements, we tried other feature selection methods, including fuzzy intersection and LASSO regression. We compared the sensitivity, specificity, and AUROC of the models. Our results suggest that a simpler two-protein with DERM and IgD as predictors can achieve comparable or slightly better predictive performance than more complex models.

## Dataset

In this module, we used two datasets: `biomarker-raw.csv`, the raw data, and `biomarker-clean.csv`, the processed data. The data is publicly available and was obtained from Hewitson *et al.* (2021). *Blood biomarker discovery for autism spectrum disorder: A proteomic analysis.* The raw dataset contains 156 observations and their levels of 1,317 proteins. All participants were boys aged 18 months to 8 years. The dataset also indicates if each participant is diagnosed with ASD (ASD) or is not diagnosed with ASD (TD). In our data, 76 participants are diagnosed with ASD and 78 are not.

The cleaned dataset also has observations from 154 participants. Each observation includes protein measurements for the proteins, although these values have been standardized. Unlike the raw data, protein values in the cleaned dataset can be negative or positive. Along with participant groups (ASD/TD), the cleaned dataset includes participants' ADOS number if they are a part of the ASD group. ADOS (Autism Diagnostic Observation Schedule) is a clinical assessment used to evaluate ASD severity. In this sample, ADOS is scored between 6 and 23, with higher values indicating more sever ASD. Additionally, the cleaned dataset has shortened names for each protein and the `Group` column has been renamed to `group`.

## Summary of published analysis

Hewitson et al. (2021) investigated whether blood protein levels could be used as biomarkers to identify autism spectrum disorder (ASD). The researchers collected blood samples from 154 male pediatric subjects from the ages of 18 months to 8 years. 76 participants were diagnosed with ASD and 78 were not. The participants with ASD were assessed using ADOS (Autism Diagnostic Observation Schedule), which evaluates ASD severity. A total of 1,317 proteins were initially measured. The SOMAScan platform was used for analysis. 192 proteins failed quality control and were subsequently removed from the analysis for a total of 1,125 proteins. The protein abundance data was normalized using a log10 transformation as well as a z-transformation. Any z-transformed values that fell outside the \[-3, 3\] range were cut in order to control for outliers. To select the proteins that would be used for model, they used random-forest, t-test, and correlation methods.

The top predictive proteins were selected from each method. There were 5 proteins in-common between each method that were selected as 'core' proteins (DERM, MAPK14, IgD, EPHB2, and suPAR). Using logistic regression, additional proteins were added to increase the model's predictive capability. Ultimately, the researchers identified nine proteins (core proteins, ROR1, GI24, elF-4H, and ARSB). They evaluated the model's performance using ROC curve (AUC), sensitivity, and specificity. They also examined correlations between the selected proteins and participant ADOS scores; The resulting protein panel achieved an AUC of approximately 0.86 (sensitivity 83%; specificity 84%), suggesting that blood protein levels may be useful for identifying ASD, although the reseatchers emphasized the need for more validation using larger, independent datasets.

## Findings

### Impact of preprocessing and outliers

In Task 1, we cleaned the raw dataset by removing the first row of protein abbreviations and changing the protein values to numeric types. We then plotted the protein levels of four proteins (CHIP, CEBPB, NSE, and PIAS4). From the four histograms, we can observe that there is right-skewness in all four proteins. The E3 Ubiquitin protein (CHIP) plot peaks between 0-5,000 followed by a gap, and then a few observations between 30,000-35,000. The CCAAT Enhancer Binding protein (CEBPB) plot shows observations are concentrated between 500-3,000 with a peak between 1,000-1,500. There is also a gap followed by a few observations between 6,000-6,500. The Gamma Enolase (NSE) plot shows observations forming a right skew from 500-3,000. The peak occurs between the 500-1,000. The E3 SUMO protein (PIAS4) plot peaks between 500-1,500 with small observations concentrating between 1,500-2,000, 2,500-3,000, 3,500-4,000, and 6,500-7,000. By log-transforming the protein levels, we can compress the larger values in our data, reducing the right-skewness and lowering the influence of larger observations. This helps with data analysis, as well as making a more symmetrical curve.

In Task 2, we removed the outlier trimming from the preprocessed data in order to analyze the outlying values. We examined the number of protein measurements more than 3 standard deviations from the mean for each subject. Subject 154 (TD) had the most with 157. Of the 10 subjects with the highest outlier counts, 7 belonged to TD group. The TD group also had a higher mean outlier count than the ASD group, although both groups had the same median of 8.5.

### Methodological variations

In Task 3, we investigated whether modifying the feature selection process would improve the performance of our model. First, we split the dataset into a testing and training set. We then applied t-tests and random forest to the training data and selected proteins appearing in the top 10 of both methods. This produced a four-protein panel (DERM, IgD, TSP4, and FSTL1), compared to the five-protein benchmark. The new model achieved the same accuracy (0.774), a slightly lower sensitivity (0.750), a higher specificity (0.800), and a slightly lower AUROC (0.871).

Next, we tried two alternative feature selection approaches. First, we increased the number of top proteins considered from each method (k = 10, 15, 20, 30, and 50). We then tested a fuzzy intersection approach, which selected proteins ranking in the top k of one method and highly in the other. Both approaches achieved their highest accuracy (0.839) with a five-protein panel that added PTN to the four proteins selected previously. However, larger panels generally performed worse. This suggests the models were overfit.

In the end, we found that including more proteins into our model did not increase performance, and DERM and IgD were the strongest predictors of ASD. While the alternative feature selection methods improved accuracy in some cases, none of the models exceeded the benchmark AUROC of 0.883. Since all models were evaluated on a single test set of 31 participants, additional cross-validation would be necessary to determine whether these differences are reliable.

### Improved classifier

In Task 4, we investigated whether a simpler model could achieve similar performance to the in-class model and if we could build a more accurate model using any method. For our simple model, we selected two proteins as our predictors, DERM and IgD, since they were the most statistically significant. To evaluate the simple model's performance, we measured its sensitivity, specificity, and AUROC, and compared the values to our benchmark. The two-protein model achieved an identical specificity, sensitivity, and accuracy score. The AUROC for the simple model (0.850) was slightly smaller than the benchmark (0.883). Since we were only able to test the simple model on 31 observations, these results could come down to luck. However, our results show that DERM and IgD are the strongest predictors from the original model.

To build our more accurate model, we used LASSO regression to select our predictors from the full panel of 1,317 proteins. We evaluated the performance of two LASSO models, one with 46 proteins and one with 17 proteins. Both achieved higher AUROC (0.913 and 0.908) and specificity (0.933 and 0.867) than the benchmark. However, both LASSO models had lower accuracy and sensitivity. This suggests that they were less effective at correctly identifying children with ASD.

To further each model, we used cross-validation. LASSO continued to achieve higher AUROC (0.819) and specificity (0.778) compared to the benchmark, but lower accuracy (0.708) and sensitivity (0.667). Our simple model, achieved the highest accuracy (0.744) and sensitivity (0.775) out of all the models. Overall, adding more proteins as predictors resulted in overfitting, as well as lower accuracy and sensitivity. Our recommended model is the simple 2-protein model.
